paper_metadata.title: Enhanced high-temperature ductility without strength drop in a lean Co Ni-based superalloy

evidence.quote: Ni-based superalloy
The present study has developed a modified, economically feasible variant of the IN738LC superalloy, demonstrating enhanced high-temperature elongation properties.

Two 5 kg ingots of IN738LC and Mo-IN738LC alloys were fabricated by vacuum induction melting.
The microstructure analysis of the two alloys revealed that the γ’ precipitates were uniformly distributed, but their size in the Mo-IN738LC alloy was larger (~21%) than that in the IN738LC alloy.

The Mo-IN738LC alloy exhibits enhanced mechanical properties, including high-temperature elongation compared to the IN738LC alloy. This is achieved by reducing expensive Co (~ 50%) content and increasing cheaper Mo (~20%) content, which reduces the overall material cost.

the addition of Al and Ti forms γ’ Ni3(Al, Ti) precipitates, which act as a crucial strengthening component

Since the Co and Mo are not the main carbide former, whereas work solution strengthening, on the other hand, an increment of a slight amount of Mo will lead to more carbide former, which will surely help in the overall strengthening of alloy as reported in previous literature [31,37].

Furthermore, a substantial density of coherent L1 2 γ’ precipitates is uniformly dispersed within the FCC matrix. These L1 2 γ’ precipitates exhibit thermal stability at elevated temperatures, thereby augmenting the strength of IN738LC via precipitation strengthening.

As dislo - cations transition from the relatively softer FCC matrix to the harder L12 γ’ precipitate, they accumulate at the interface, giving rise to substantial back stress. This back stress, in turn, counteracts applied shear stresses, resulting in a significantly elevated apparent strength for FCC matrix.
Mo is one of the most sought elements to reduce SFE (~0.04 mol fraction addition) it causes the formation of twins, which inhibits dislocation motion, which leads to strengthening [33].
Reducing the size of twins to the nanoscale accentuates the interaction between twin boundaries and dislocations, resulting in heightened strain hardening and plastic deformation [42–44].
